newsitem.title: INDIA: Murky politics sends shiver through Indian stocks.
newsitem.headline: Murky politics sends shiver through Indian stocks.

text.p: Wary Indian investors kept a low profile on Monday driving share prices down in jittery trade as the political picture turned murky ahead of a crucial confidence vote later this week, analysts said.
Bombay's benchmark index slid 20.40 points, or 0.6 percent, to 3529.97 in afternoon trade. Shares on the Delhi and Calcutta bourses fell in nervous, low volumes.
"The uncertainty is increasing rather than decreasing," said Subra Subramanian, director at securities firm H.G. Asia. "This weekend has not helped much."

Congress President Sitaram Kesri who sparked a political crisis on March 30 when he abruptly withdrew support to the United Front government, launched a scathing attack on Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda over the weekend.
Kesri told supporters on Saturday that though he did not hold a "grudge" against the ruling coalition, he viewed Deve Gowda as "not only inefficient but communal."

"Last week it seemed like we were looking to some kind of solution but the latest noises show that people are adopting very hardline positions," said Anand Aithal, India strategist at Goldman Sachs & Co in Hong Kong.
Analysts said reports that the opposition Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) may vote against the government in a key confidence vote due on April 11 had thickened the political fog.
The BJP is the single largest party in the 542-member lower house of parliament with 162 deputies.
"If everyone in parliament votes against everyone else, we are bound to see fresh elections," Aithal said, adding that whatever the outcome investor confidence would be hit.
"Even if general elections are avoided, investors are unlikely to become complacent in a hurry."
Aithal said cyclicals like cement and steel were most likely to be hit in the event of prolonged political uncertainty.
Analysts said last week's decision to bar foreign airlines from taking stakes in the domestic sector sent another worrisome signal about the pace of economic reforms.
A direct casualty of the new rule is a proposed tie-up between India's largest business group, the Tatas, and Singapore Airlines, to set up a $600 million domestic network.
"The Tata-SIA decision was ignored to some extent because of the political mess but it's definitely at the back of people's minds," said the chief dealer at a UK-based brokerage.
"How can you plan for future investments if the rules keep changing?"
HG Asia's Subramanian said economic reforms were likely to take a backseat until the political turmoil subsided.
"Most ministers will have very little time to do anything except retain power. All economic decisions will probably be postponed," he said.
Analysts said the political uncertainty would keep cautious investors on the sidelines this week.
"Things are so much in the air -- the market will trade in a dead zone this week," the chief dealer said.
-- Bombay newsroom, (91) 22-265 9000
